title: AI Built For Law Outperforms ChatGPT, Claude, And Gemini On Legal Reasoning Benchmark
author: LawSites / LawNext

dom.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source shares the cluster’s concern that fluent or correct-looking answers can conceal unsound legal reasoning and supports standardized, reproducible evaluation. However, it evaluates rule identification and factual application through bar-exam questions and vendor/model comparisons rather than specific professional legal work products, so it redirects evaluation toward richer exam-based reasoning measures rather than the cluster’s central task-specific professional benchmark approach.
qs: The study measured not just whether each system chose the correct answer, but whether the legal reasoning behind it was sound: Did it identify the right rule?

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by presenting strong results for a purpose-built system on a narrow bar-question benchmark while explicitly qualifying what those results establish. Its vendor-run design, judge-model scoring, possible training-data exposure and evidence of persuasive errors in other models reinforce the need for task-specific interpretation, benchmark scrutiny and human verification rather than claims of dependable autonomous lawyering.
qs: As with any benchmark using a commercially available question set, training data exposure cannot be ruled out for any evaluated system, including DescrybeLM.*  When general-purpose models were wrong, they were confidently wrong.
Among 52 incorrect outputs, 49 delivered assertive, well-structured reasoning that did not signal uncertainty — the failure mode that imposes the highest verification burden on legal practitioners.

kp.k: Vendor benchmark reports purpose-built legal AI outperforming general models
kp.d: The March 2026 article reports Descrybe's launch of DescrybeLM and its vendor-produced benchmark of 200 multistate bar exam questions. DescrybeLM answered 200 correctly (100%), compared with ChatGPT 5.2's 187 (93.5%), Claude Opus 4.5's 177 (88.5%), and Gemini 3 Pro's 184 (92.0%). Reported rubric-scored reasoning quality was 99.70%, 93.41%, 89.03%, and 91.45%, respectively. These are reported benchmark results, rather than findings about performance across legal practice generally.
qs: Descrybe ran a controlled benchmark against ChatGPT 5.2, Claude Opus 4.5, and Gemini 3 Pro on 200 multistate bar exam questions.

kp.k: Benchmark assesses rule identification and application under standardized conditions
kp.d: The study used the NCBE MBE Complete Practice Exam, Questions 1–200 without exclusions, under standardized conditions without external web access. The article reports 800 separate evaluation runs with blinded scoring. Assessment covered both answer correctness and reasoning, including identifying the appropriate legal rule and applying it to the facts.
qs: All four systems were tested under standardized, no-external-web benchmark conditions using the NCBE MBE Complete Practice Exam (Questions 1–200, no exclusions), producing 800 separate evaluation runs with blinded scoring.

The study measured not just whether each system chose the correct answer, but whether the legal reasoning behind it was sound: Did it identify the right rule? Apply it correctly to the facts? Avoid the traps that produce persuasive but wrong analysis?

kp.k: Judge-model scoring and possible training exposure qualify results
kp.d: The document explicitly qualifies reasoning-quality scores as judge-model assessments and states that prior training exposure to the commercially available questions cannot be ruled out for any system, including DescrybeLM. Descrybe CEO Kara Peterson presents the study as testing the company's thesis about purpose-built legal AI, acknowledges that vendor-produced benchmarks warrant scrutiny, and invites replication using the published methodology.
qs: Rubric-scored reasoning quality reflects judge-model scoring; see Evaluation Approach within the white paper for methodology and limitations.
As with any benchmark using a commercially available question set, training data exposure cannot be ruled out for any evaluated system, including DescrybeLM.
We know that vendor-produced benchmarks invite scrutiny — as they should, that's why we published our methodology and invite anyone to replicate it.

kp.k: Confident legal errors increase practitioners' verification burden
kp.d: Among 52 incorrect general-purpose model outputs, the article reports that 49 contained assertive, well-structured reasoning without signaling uncertainty. The dominant errors were choosing the wrong legal standard or misapplying the correct standard. The article characterizes apparently competent but incorrect analysis as the most dangerous failure mode and the one imposing the highest human verification burden on legal practitioners.
qs: Among 52 incorrect outputs, 49 delivered assertive, well-structured reasoning that did not signal uncertainty — the failure mode that imposes the highest verification burden on legal practitioners.
The dominant patterns were applying the wrong legal standard or misapplying the correct one, while the prose read like competent analysis.

kp.k: Confident tone does not reliably indicate answer correctness
kp.d: The scoring log reportedly flagged overconfident tone in correct as well as incorrect outputs from Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 Pro. DescrybeLM and ChatGPT 5.2 each received zero overconfidence flags across 200 outputs. The article argues that tone alone cannot provide practitioners a reliable correctness signal when a system sounds equally confident in right and wrong answers.
qs: The scoring log also revealed that two general-purpose models — Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 Pro — exhibited overconfident tone on correct outputs, not only incorrect ones.
DescrybeLM and ChatGPT 5.2 each received zero overconfidence flags across all 200 outputs.
A system that sounds equally confident whether it is right or wrong gives practitioners no reliable signal from tone alone.

kp.k: Article cautions against relying on cross-model checking
kp.d: Across the 200 questions, at least one general-purpose model missed 40 questions, two or more missed 11, and all three missed only 1. The article describes the errors as largely unpredictable and non-overlapping and presents these results as showing that cross-checking general-purpose models is not a reliable substitute for an initially correct answer.
qs: The study also found that cross-checking between general-purpose models is not a reliable substitute for getting the answer right the first time.
Across 200 questions, 40 were missed by at least one model, 11 were missed by two or more, and only 1 was missed by all three — meaning errors were largely unpredictable and non-overlapping.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article reports that purpose-built DescrybeLM outperformed three general-purpose models on a legal-reasoning benchmark, and claims that confidently wrong general-purpose outputs increase practitioners' verification burden.
pts.d: The article presents comparative performance on legal exam questions as evidence of a meaningful difference between specialized and general-purpose AI for legal reasoning. Descrybe CEO Kara Peterson describes this as the company's thesis and frames published benchmark evidence as support for legal professionals' tool-selection decisions. The article further claims that authoritative-sounding answers can conceal use of the wrong legal standard or incorrect application of the right standard; tone alone is therefore not a reliable correctness signal. It also claims that cross-checking between general-purpose models is not a reliable substitute for an initially correct answer. These are current capability and workflow claims, not predictions about employment, pricing or firm structure.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is Descrybe's own controlled benchmark of 200 MBE questions, with blinded scoring and judge-model assessment of reasoning quality.
pts.d: The article reports 800 evaluation runs across four systems using the NCBE MBE Complete Practice Exam, Questions 1–200 without exclusions. DescrybeLM answered 200/200 correctly with 99.70% rubric-scored reasoning quality; ChatGPT 5.2 answered 187/200 with 93.41%; Claude Opus 4.5 answered 177/200 with 89.03%; Gemini 3 Pro answered 184/200 with 91.45%. The article reports assertive reasoning without uncertainty in 49 of the 52 incorrect general-purpose outputs. It separately reports overconfidence flags on correct outputs for Claude and Gemini, and zero overconfidence flags across all 200 outputs for each of DescrybeLM and ChatGPT. Its cross-checking claim draws on error overlap: 40 questions missed by at least one general-purpose model, 11 by two or more, and one by all three. The evidence is a vendor-produced benchmark rather than a reported study of deployed legal-service outcomes; the CEO acknowledges the need for scrutiny and invites replication.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern capabilities at DescrybeLM's March 2026 launch under specified exam-benchmark conditions, with an explicit possible training-exposure qualification.
pts.d: The article announces the launch and white paper as occurring 'Today' in its March 2026 publication context. Its numerical comparisons concern the named model versions on a fixed, commercially available 200-question exam under standardized conditions without external web access. Reasoning-quality percentages are judge-model scores subject to the white paper's methodology and limitations. The article expressly states that training exposure to the questions cannot be ruled out for any system, including DescrybeLM. It gives no future adoption timeline or quantified projection of effects on actual legal practice.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The stated affected group is legal professionals selecting AI tools and checking AI-generated legal analysis.
pts.d: Peterson frames the benchmark as evidence for practitioners' purchasing or tool-selection decisions. The article identifies human verification of plausible but legally incorrect answers as the principal practice burden, and cautions practitioners against relying on confident tone or cross-model checks as substitutes for correctness. It does not identify distinct effects for particular firm sizes, practice areas, in-house departments, clients or underserved populations, nor does it claim quantified time or cost savings.
